Topic:Public Schools

Thu 2 Jul 2026 at 9:06am

Catherine Mayfield says the issue deserves urgent attention. (ABC Great Southern: Astrid Volzke )

Parents say not enough is being done to address the ongoing issue of asbestos being found in Hyden Primary School's playground.

The most recent incident was in June this year, with the area cordoned off.

The Department of Education says a further assessment will be conducted during the July school holidays.

Parents of children attending Hyden Primary School in regional Western Australia say not enough is being done to address the ongoing problem of asbestos being found in the playground, sometimes by children.

Catherine Mayfield, president of the parents and citizens association, said locals and students at the school had been finding pieces of asbestos for at least 12 years.

"They notify the teachers, who then notify the education department, which is based in Narrogin, so they send someone out, remove the piece of asbestos, and basically they just continue."

Under the Department of Education policy, the area is taped off until the asbestos-containing material is removed.

Students have previously dug up asbestos. (ABC Great Southern: Astrid Volzke )

Asbestos Disease Society of Australia chief executive Melita Markey said more should be done to protect the students and staff at the school.

"My view on the matter is it should be properly sealed with proper cover, the contaminated areas, and then over the holidays appropriately removed," she said.

"All children are precious, and we should be taking everything in our power to prevent any exposure."

Krystie Falconer, the mother of three children who have attended the school, said one of the areas where asbestos was found was a garden used by students.

"One time they were digging down to plant seed and some [asbestos] was found," she said.

Hyden Primary School is about 330 kilometres south-east of Perth. (ABC Great Southern: Astrid Volzke )

She said it was not a recent issue.

"You talk to past students that lived here 20 years ago, and they were digging up asbestos then.

"That's a long potential exposure."

Letters sent to WA Education Minister Sabine Winton from parents called for a full assessment and the urgent removal of contaminated materials.

"We are aware of the department policy, however we do not feel that the policies are acceptable given the health and safety nature of this hazard," the letters said.

It also speaks to concerns from gardening and maintenance staff about working in the area due to the potential presence of further asbestos materials.

Catherine Mayfield says students and staff have been finding asbestos in the playground for at least 12 years. (ABC Great Southern: Astrid Volzke)

Ms Mayfield said there had been no response to the letters.

She said the asbestos that was being uncovered was believed to have come from an asbestos ablution block that was buried on the grounds.

"We think, over time with erosion and kids digging in the garden, that it has exposed asbestos, and it's exposed it for years and years now, but it seems to be coming up more frequently over time," she said.

The most recent incident occurred in June.

A Department of Education spokesperson said the department was aware asbestos-containing material had been identified at the school.

"In accordance with department procedures, the material has been removed and sent for testing and identification, and the area has been cordoned off to prevent students from entering," they said.

"As a precautionary measure, further assessment of the site will take place during the July school holidays to identify any further actions required."

They said the school had raised the issue of asbestos-containing material with the department four times.

Melita Markey says asbestos exposure in WA schools is an outgoing issue. (Supplied)

Hyden is located about 330 kilometres south-east of Perth, and Ms Mayfield said they feel forgotten.

"We just feel like out here, because there's fewer children involved, it's just a constant bandaid solution, and it's not rectifying the actual problem," she said.
